1366.title: Order and effort
1366.hook: all is within the hukam, yet the Gurus ask us to strive
1366.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Japji Sahib, which says all are within the hukam, each morning, and they hold honest work, kirat karo, alongside remembering the Name and sharing as part of daily Sikh life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Nanak's aarti: the sky as the tray, and the light in everything. Your line: beyond and within. A new week starts.

A farmer in Punjab can't make it rain. She can't choose the heat, or the day the monsoon arrives, or whether a storm flattens the wheat a week before harvest. And still, every season, she's up before light: plowing, sowing, watering, mending the channel where the water runs. Nobody would call her lazy for not controlling the sky, and nobody would call her wise for sitting in the doorway waiting for it. Sikh thought takes her life seriously as a question: if everything happens within God's order, why try?
screen: `SHE CAN'T MAKE IT RAIN.` → `UP BEFORE LIGHT, EVERY SEASON.` → `IF ALL IS ORDERED, WHY TRY?`

segments.voice: Hukam is the Granth's word for the order: the command, the will, the way the One runs everything. In year one you met it as living in tune. In the second pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: by hukam all forms are made; by hukam some are high and some low, some get joy and some get pain. Then the line that leaves no gaps: everyone is within the hukam, and no one is outside it. And yet the same scripture is full of work. Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: make the effort, and earning by it, live in peace; meditating, you meet the Lord. Sikh life is built on this. Kirat karo, earn an honest living, is one of the pillars Sikhs name beside remembering the Name and sharing. How do the two fit? Sikh teachers say hukam isn't fate in the sense of a script you sit and watch. It's closer to the farmer's sky: the frame you live inside. Your effort is part of the order, not a fight against it. Japji's answer to how to live is, in paraphrase, to walk in the way of the hukam. Walking is still walking; you still lift your feet. That takes a weight off. If everything hung on your effort alone, every failure would be total. If nothing did, there'd be no reason to get up. Within the order, you do your part fully, and let the rest be what it is. Strive within the order.
screen: `HUKAM: NO ONE IS OUTSIDE IT.` · `MAKE THE EFFORT, LIVE IN PEACE.` · `NOT A SCRIPT, A SKY TO WORK UNDER.` · `DO YOUR PART; LET THE REST BE.` · then, large: `STRIVE WITHIN THE ORDER.`

segments.voice: Bring one worry to mind and gently split it in two: the part that's yours, a call, a task, an apology, and the part that isn't, other people's choices, the weather, the outcome. Choose one small piece from your side, and with each out-breath set the other side down.
Order and effort. Everything is within the hukam, and still the Gurus ask for honest work and striving: your effort is part of the order. Today's word.
Your line: strive within the order. The sky isn't yours; the plowing is. See you tomorrow.

1367.title: The robe and the door
1367.hook: deeds shape the body we are given; grace opens the door
1367.carry: deeds shape the robe; grace opens the door
1367.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning, including the line about deeds and the robe, grace and the door, and Sikh life joins seva and honest work with remembrance and trust in the Guru's grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, order and effort: everyone within the hukam, and still the Gurus ask us to strive. Your line: strive within the order.

Two words side by side in the fourth pauri of Japji: karmi, nadri. In paraphrase, the line runs: by deeds comes the robe; by grace, the door of liberation. A robe and a door. An odd pair for one breath. A robe is something you're wrapped in every day; it takes the shape of you. A door is something you can stand in front of for a very long time and never open with your own hand. Today's word is the first half: karam.
screen: `A ROBE AND A DOOR.` → `KARMI, NADRI.` → `TODAY'S WORD: THE FIRST HALF.`

segments.voice: The robe first. Sikh readers take the robe in this line as the body, the life we're given. Karam is deeds, actions and their weight. What we have done shapes what we carry: the body, the circumstances, the habits that wrap around us. On its own, that would be a strict ledger. Then the door. Nadar is the glance, the gracious look of the One. The line says the door of liberation opens by nadar, not by karam. You can do good for a lifetime, and the door still isn't something you buy. It is given. Why both? If the line said only deeds, life would be bookkeeping, and anyone behind would stay behind. If it said only grace, there'd be no reason to do good at all. Guru Nanak keeps both: deeds really do shape us, and the last step is a gift. The same pauri closes, in paraphrase: the True One is all of it. Readers hold the line in two ways. Some Sikh interpreters read karmi itself as grace, so the robe, too, would be a gift. Others read it as deeds, as today does. Both readings keep grace at the door. So the life this points to looks like yesterday's farmer: do the good in front of you with your whole heart, and leave the door to the giver. Deeds and grace.

segments.voice: Picture one good deed within reach today, carrying something for someone, a kind word to a coworker, a bill paid fairly, and see yourself doing it. Let the picture end the moment the deed is done, and let the result belong to someone else. If you pray, let that letting go become a hope for grace; if you don't, just feel the difference between doing and receiving.
Karam. Deeds, actions and their weight: in Japji, by deeds comes the robe, and by grace, nadar, the door of liberation. Today's word.
Your line: deeds shape the robe; grace opens the door. That's today, done.

1368.title: The long round of births
1368.hook: the Granth speaks of many lives and the chance this human life is
1368.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib in the evening, which includes Guru Arjan's line that this human body is the turn to meet the Lord of the universe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karam: by deeds comes the robe, by grace the door. Your line: deeds and grace.

In the evening, in homes and gurdwaras, Sikhs pray Rehras. Partway through comes a line that sounds less like a hymn than a tap on the shoulder. In paraphrase: you have been given this human body; this is your turn to meet the Lord of the universe. Your turn. Like a number called at a counter after a long wait. The line assumes a long line, a queue of lives before this one. It doesn't argue for it. It just turns, looks you in the eye, and says: now.
screen: `A LINE IN THE EVENING PRAYER.` → `THIS IS YOUR TURN.` → `NOW.`

segments.voice: Behind the line is the long round. The Granth speaks of the soul passing through many lives and many forms: in some hymns, as a worm, a bird, a tree, a stone, round and round. It doesn't linger on the details. The round is the background, the long road behind. The hymn in Rehras is by Guru Arjan, and its point is the human life: the turn, the moment the door can open. Sikh teachers add that of all the forms in the round, this is the one that can remember the Name on purpose. What is the turn for? The same hymn says, in paraphrase: your other tasks are of no use here; join the company of the holy and dwell on the Name alone. That sounds stern, but it's about priority, not about quitting work. The farmer still farms. The line asks what the farming is for. Why does this matter on a Tuesday? If you believe in many lives, the line makes this one precious: don't waste the turn. If you don't, it still lands: this life is the one in your hands, and today is part of it. Either way, the Guru isn't trying to frighten anyone with the long round. He's pointing at the counter where your number just came up. This life is the chance.

segments.voice: Feel your hands, your feet, the weight of your body on the seat: this body, this one, and today happening once. Let one thing come to mind you'd be sorry to leave undone, a call, a moment of attention, a word of thanks. If you pray, offer the day as your turn; if not, sit with the plain fact that you're alive right now.
The long round of births. The Granth's picture of many lives and many forms, and the human life as the turn: the chance to meet the One. Today's word.

1369.title: Free while living
1369.hook: liberation is possible in this life, not only after
1369.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib, which describes the one who takes the Lord's will to heart as free while living, and Sikh teaching places that freedom inside family life, work and service, not apart from them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long round of births, and Guru Arjan's line: this human body is your turn. Your line: this life is the chance.

Liberation sounds like something at the end: a gate at the far side of a long road, a reward after the last breath. Yesterday's lesson could even be heard that way: this life is the turn, so the prize comes after. But Sikh scripture has a phrase that turns that picture inside out. Two words, jivan mukat. Free while living. Not free someday. Free while you still have a job, a family, a phone that won't stop buzzing. What could that look like on a weekday?
screen: `A GATE AT THE END OF THE ROAD?` → `JIVAN MUKAT.` → `FREE WHILE YOU STILL HAVE A JOB.`

segments.voice: Jivan means life, living. Mukat means freed, released. Together: one who is liberated while alive. The Granth uses it of people walking around in the world, not only of souls after death. In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: the one who takes the Lord's will to heart is called free while living. To that person, joy and sorrow are alike; there is lasting bliss, and no separation. Notice what's missing. It doesn't say the free person has no sorrow. It says sorrow and joy weigh the same. The storms still come. They just don't knock the person off the ground. Freedom from what? Not from the world. Sikh life stays in it: family, work, langar, sangat. The freedom is from being pushed around inside, by ego, by fear, by the endless wanting more. It ties the week together. Order and effort: you work, and accept the hukam. Deeds and grace: you do good and leave the door to the One. A person who can actually live like that, here, is what jivan mukat names. If freedom came only after death, there'd be nothing to taste now. Jivan mukat says the taste is here, in this life, even in a hard week, even a moment at a time. Free now.

segments.voice: Let one good thing from this week sit in front of you, then set one hard thing beside it. Don't push the hard one away or hold on to the good one; let them sit side by side, the same weight, while you keep breathing. If you pray, hold both as within the will; if you don't, notice the breath going on underneath both.
Free while living. Jivan mukat: liberated in this life, not only after it, where joy and sorrow weigh the same. Today's word.

1370.title: The realm of truth
1370.hook: Sach Khand is described as the home of the Formless, the goal of the path
1370.tomorrow: The five realms as a path
1370.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning, ending with the realms that lead to Sach Khand, the realm of truth where the Formless One dwells.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jivan mukat: free while living, where joy and sorrow weigh the same. Your line: free now.

Near the end of Japji, the morning prayer, Guru Nanak describes a series of realms, khands, like rooms opening one into the next. Tomorrow walks the whole series. Today goes straight to the last room. And something strange happens there. After stanza upon stanza of description, Guru Nanak stops and admits that describing this place is hard. Hard like iron. The poet who has named worlds upon worlds reaches the realm of truth and says plainly that words strain here.
screen: `REALMS, LIKE ROOMS.` → `STRAIGHT TO THE LAST ONE.` → `HARD LIKE IRON TO DESCRIBE.`

segments.voice: Sach is truth; khand is a realm, a region. Sach Khand, the realm of truth. You reached it once before, near the end of year one's walk through the Japji. Japji says, in paraphrase: in the realm of truth dwells the Formless One, Nirankar. Creating, the One watches over the creation, and blesses it with the glance of grace. That's nadar, the glance we met with the robe and the door. Here it isn't one look at one person. It's the One gazing on everything made, with joy. The pauri says there are worlds there, and continents and universes beyond counting; try to count them, and there'd be no end. Form upon form, all moving as the hukam moves them, and the One sees them and is glad. Here the week's threads meet: the order everything lives within, the grace that opens the door, the Formless One beyond and within. Sikh readers take Sach Khand as the goal of the path, the home of the Formless. Some read it as a place the soul reaches; some as a state of union lived even now, which links it back to yesterday's free while living. Then the honest end. In paraphrase: to describe this, Nanak says, is as hard as iron. The text holds the door open, and admits it can't fully describe the room. Home in truth.
screen: `SACH KHAND: THE REALM OF TRUTH.` · `HOME OF THE FORMLESS.` · `WORLDS BEYOND COUNTING, IN THE HUKAM.` · `HARD AS IRON TO DESCRIBE.` · then, large: `HOME IN TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Let the words in your head slow down, the way the Guru's words slowed at the edge of this realm, and when a thought comes, let it pass without naming it. If you pray, rest in being seen by a gracious glance; if you don't, rest in what's true right now: this breath, this room, nothing to add.
The realm of truth. Sach Khand, which Japji calls the home of the Formless One, where creation is watched with grace, and which Guru Nanak says is as hard as iron to describe. Today's word.
Your line: home in truth. Some rooms are bigger than any words. See you tomorrow.

1371.title: The five realms as a path
1371.word: The five realms as a path
1371.hook: duty, knowledge, effort, grace, truth: a map of growth
1371.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning, and its closing pauris describe the realms of duty, knowledge, effort, grace and truth, which Sikh teachers explain as stages of spiritual growth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sach Khand, the realm of truth, as hard as iron to describe. Your line: home in truth.

A trail map at the foot of a mountain has a red dot on it: you are here. Without the dot, the map is just a pretty drawing. With it, you can see how far you've come and what's next. Yesterday jumped straight to the top of a mountain in Japji. Today goes back to the trailhead and walks the whole thing. Sikh readers have read Guru Nanak's realms as stages of growth, a map of the inner climb. And the map asks: where's your dot?
screen: `YOU ARE HERE.` → `BACK TO THE TRAILHEAD.` → `WHERE'S YOUR DOT?`

segments.voice: Duty comes first: Dharam Khand. Japji says, in paraphrase, that amid nights and seasons and days, wind, water and fire, the earth was set as a home for dharma, right living. Here deeds are weighed, each judged by what it does. It's the ground floor. Then knowledge: Gian Khand, where, Japji says, knowledge blazes, opening on a universe without edges, worlds and suns and beings beyond count. Readers take that vastness as cutting the ego down to size. Then effort: Saram Khand, whose language, Japji says, is beauty; there the mind and understanding are shaped and refined. Readers differ on saram: some hear effort, some beauty, some humility. All three describe a self being worked on, like a craftsman's piece on the bench. Then Karam Khand, whose language is power: here live warriors filled with the One's strength. Here karam is read as grace, the other reading of the word we met with the robe and the door. And last, Sach Khand, home of the Formless. Duty, knowledge, effort, grace, truth. Readers notice a turn at the fourth step: in their reading, the climber stops climbing and is carried. Effort gets you up the slope, they say, and grace takes you over the ridge. Some Sikh readers stress that the realms aren't a ladder you finish, but rooms you may move between on any day. Either way, the map is for one honest question. Where am I.
screen: `DHARAM KHAND: DUTY, DEEDS WEIGHED.` · `GIAN KHAND: KNOWLEDGE BLAZES.` · `SARAM KHAND: THE SELF SHAPED.` · `KARAM AND SACH: GRACE, THEN TRUTH.` · then, large: `WHERE AM I.`

segments.voice: Walk the realms slowly in your mind, asking without grading yourself: am I doing what's right in front of me, do I remember how big the world is, am I letting myself be shaped, am I leaving room to be carried? Notice which room feels like where you stand today, and breathe there for a while.
The five realms as a path. Dharam, gian, saram, karam and sach: duty, knowledge, effort, grace and truth, read by Sikh teachers as a map of the inner climb. Today's word.

1372.title: Ego is not you
1372.hook: haumai is a veil, not the self; the Gurus never ask for self-hatred
1372.howItsDone: Sikhs describe haumai, ego, as the wall or illness that separates a person from the One, and look to the Guru's Word and remembrance of the Name to heal it, rather than to self-punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five realms as a path: duty, knowledge, effort, grace, truth. Your line: where am I.

A bathroom mirror after a hot shower, fogged over. Nobody looks at the gray blur and says, well, I suppose I'm fog now. You wipe once, and there you are. The face was there the whole time; the fog was only on the glass. Yesterday's map leaves a question: what keeps a person from climbing? The Granth's answer has a name, haumai, ego. And the Gurus talk about it more like fog on a mirror than a stain on a soul.
screen: `A MIRROR FULL OF FOG.` → `WIPE ONCE: THERE YOU ARE.` → `HAUMAI: FOG, NOT FACE.`

segments.voice: Haumai is the Granth's word for ego: the voice that says I, me, mine, and puts itself at the center of every room. In year one you met it as the disease with its own cure; today asks what it isn't. In the first stanza of the Japji comes a question. In paraphrase: how does a person become true, and how is the wall of falsehood torn down? Guru Nanak's answer: walk in the hukam, the divine order. Haumai is a wall between a person and the One, and a wall can come down. Nobody says the wall is the house. What's underneath? In Sohila, in the line we met in his aarti, Guru Nanak says that in everyone there is a light, and that light is the One's. So when the fog clears, what's waiting is not something rotten. It is light. And in Asa di Var, a salok of Guru Angad calls haumai a long and deep illness, then says the medicine is within it too: by grace, a person lives the Guru's Word. Nobody hates a friend for having a fever. You bring soup, call the doctor, wait with them. The Granth treats ego as something to heal, and the healing is remembering, not punishing. So a Sikh who catches their own pride isn't asked to despise themselves. Self-hatred, if you listen closely, can be haumai wearing a sadder coat: still I, still me, still the center of the room. Not self-hatred.
screen: `HAUMAI: I, ME, MINE.` · `A WALL THAT CAN COME DOWN.` · `UNDERNEATH: THE ONE'S LIGHT.` · `AN ILLNESS WITH ITS CURE INSIDE.` · then, large: `NOT SELF-HATRED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you did lately that you're not proud of, and notice the voice that shows up to talk about it: is it fair, is it loud? Set it down, and speak to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend with a fever: that happened, you can make it right, you are more than this. If you pray, let Waheguru come gently on each breath.
Ego is not you. Haumai is a wall, a fog, an illness over the light, never the light itself. Today's word.
Your line: not self-hatred. If the voice against yourself ever turns to thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out now: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Go gently.
